title: How a Top Cleric’s Fatwa Could Complicate Pakistan’s Crypto Ambitions
excerpt: Mufti Taqi Usmani’s ruling that cryptocurrency is not wealth under Islamic law threatens Islamabad’s push to regulate digital assets and its “crypto diplomacy” with the Trump family’s World Liberty Financial.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Mufti Taqi Usmani's fatwa declares cryptocurrency impermissible under Shariah law.
  • Pakistan's PVARA seeks clarity on asset-backed digital instruments versus speculative tokens.
  • The ruling jeopardizes Pakistan's deal with World Liberty Financial for stablecoin payments.
  • Analysts warn the fatwa may hinder bank-led crypto adoption, but retail trading remains stable.
The Fatwa's Ripple Effect
›Mufti Taqi Usmani issued a fatwa in June 2026.
›96.35% of Pakistan's 240 million population identifies as Muslim.
›Fatwa covers Bitcoin, Ethereum, and stablecoins like USDT.
›Usmani's rulings influence Deobandi institutions in India.
›Pakistan receives over $30 billion annually in remittances.
Source: The News International, 2023 Census
  • Mufti Muhammad Taqi Usmani, one of the Islamic world’s most influential scholars, issued a fatwa in June 2026 declaring cryptocurrency impermissible under Shariah law.
  • Pakistan’s crypto regulator, PVARA, is pushing back by asking the seminary to distinguish between speculative tokens and asset-backed digital instruments like stablecoins.
  • The ruling complicates Islamabad’s deal with World Liberty Financial, the Trump family’s crypto business, to explore using its USD1 stablecoin for cross-border payments.
  • Analysts warn the fatwa could slow bank-led crypto adoption, though retail trading volumes remain unaffected so far.

A Fatwa That Rattled the Market

In June 2026, Mufti Muhammad Taqi Usmani — an 82-year-old former Supreme Court judge, president of Pakistan’s largest madrassa board Wifaq-ul-Madaris Al-Arabia, and a globally recognized authority on Islamic finance — signed a fatwa declaring that cryptocurrency does not qualify as maal (property or wealth) under Shariah. Therefore, buying and selling it is impermissible.

The ruling, issued from Jamia Darul Uloom Karachi along with five other scholars, covered the full spectrum of digital assets: Bitcoin, Ethereum, blockchain-based tokens, and stablecoins like Tether’s USDT. It stated that “using different terms such as cryptocurrency, virtual currency, token or stablecoin does not change the nature of these digital assets or alter the religious position on them.”

Usmani’s son, Hassan Usmani, confirmed the fatwa’s authenticity after it circulated on social media, according to The News International. The ruling was prompted by a specific query about purchasing books and an online course using crypto — but its implications are sweeping.

Why This Scholar Matters

In a country where 96.35% of the 240-million-strong population identifies as Muslim, according to the 2023 census, religious pronouncements on financial matters carry enormous weight. Usmani is not an ordinary cleric. Selected as the most influential Muslim personality in the world in 2020, his fatwas are widely followed by Deobandi scholars and institutions across Pakistan and beyond, including the Darul Uloom Deoband in India.

"If the scholars hold firm, Pakistan’s “crypto diplomacy” could find itself constrained not by Washington or markets, but by Karachi’s oldest seminary.</p>"

His credentials in Islamic finance specifically make this ruling potent. Usmani played a central role in developing the modern framework for sukuk (Islamic bonds) and has served on the Shariah boards of multiple international financial institutions. When he says crypto isn’t wealth, Muslim investors across South Asia listen.

“The edict as it stands could become a hurdle to broader, bank-led crypto adoption beyond Pakistan’s urban trading community.”

— Waqas Ghani, Head of Research, JS Global Capital

A Government Caught Between Crypto Diplomacy and Religious Authority

The timing of the fatwa is particularly awkward for Islamabad. Pakistan has been on a rapid crypto-embrace trajectory. The Virtual Assets Act 2026, passed in March, established the Pakistan Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (PVARA) as a statutory licensing body. In April, the State Bank of Pakistan allowed commercial banks to open accounts for licensed virtual asset service providers for the first time in eight years.

Most notably, in January 2026, Pakistan signed a memorandum of understanding with SC Financial Technologies — an affiliate of World Liberty Financial, the Trump family’s crypto venture — to explore integrating the USD1 stablecoin into Pakistan’s cross-border payment systems. The deal was signed in the presence of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and army chief General Asim Munir, underlining its diplomatic significance, according to Reuters.

Pakistan's Crypto Landscape
March 2026
Pakistan passes the Virtual Assets Act, establishing PVARA.
April 2026
State Bank allows banks to open accounts for virtual asset providers.
January 2026
Pakistan signs MoU with World Liberty Financial for USD1 stablecoin.
June 2026
Mufti Usmani issues fatwa against cryptocurrency.

Bilal bin Saqib, PVARA’s chairman, has not challenged the fatwa head-on. Instead, he met with Usmani personally and asked the seminary to draw a distinction between different categories of digital assets.

“The central question the fatwa raises is whether a digital asset constitutes recognised wealth under Shariah. That is precisely the right question, and it is why these instruments must be examined individually.”

— Bilal bin Saqib, Chairman, PVARA

Saqib argued that a blockchain-recorded sukuk represents ownership of a real, income-generating asset, while gold-backed tokens or fully reserved stablecoins carry enforceable claims on something tangible. Blockchain itself, he said, is “a record-keeping and verification technology, not a financial asset.” He acknowledged, however, that “the scholars’ concerns” about purely speculative tokens “must be taken seriously.”

Impact on the Indian Diaspora

The fatwa’s ripple effects extend beyond Pakistan’s borders. Usmani’s rulings are followed by Deobandi institutions in India, which oversee thousands of madrassas. With an estimated 20 million crypto users in India, a broad Shariah objection to digital assets could influence Muslim investors across South Asia. For diaspora communities in the Gulf states, the UK, and North America who remit money to Pakistan — the country receives over 0 billion annually in remittances — the classification of stablecoins as impermissible could affect emerging digital remittance channels.

What Happens Next

For now, the fatwa’s practical impact appears limited. Waqas Ghani of JS Global Capital told Reuters that crypto trading volumes in Pakistan have remained unaffected, likely because the country’s urban trading community treats crypto more as a speculative asset than a Shariah-compliant financial instrument.

The real test is whether PVARA can persuade the seminary to issue a more nuanced ruling that carves out space for asset-backed tokens and stablecoins. Saqib has signaled that this is his strategy. “Pakistan has the opportunity to lead the world in Shariah-compliant digital finance,” he told Reuters, “and that leadership must be built with our scholars.”

But bridging the gap between a regulatory authority racing to issue exchange licenses and a seminary that sees crypto as notional numbers — not real wealth — will require more than dialogue. If the scholars hold firm, Pakistan’s “crypto diplomacy” could find itself constrained not by Washington or markets, but by Karachi’s oldest seminary.
